note: Composite circumstances on invented blocks, drawn from documented US patterns. Loops are hypotheses. The simulator reads 'select' and each pattern's 'match' to tag records; the lens reads everything else.

blocks.name: Pelham Street
blocks.summary: Rowhouses cleared for a civic center in 1962, rooming hotels torn down in the 1980s, and rents climbing as the towers fill.

contexts.title: Urban renewal clears the Pelham rowhouses
contexts.body: A federal urban renewal grant paid the city to clear eleven blocks of rowhouses west of the courthouse for a civic center and parking. About 900 households were moved, most of them renters, and few were offered a place to come back to.

contexts.title: The rooming hotels come down
contexts.body: Downtown had four single-room hotels where a worker could rent by the week without a deposit. They were demolished for office towers in the 1980s, and nothing that cheap replaced them. The shelter on Pelham opened in 1988.

contexts.title: Rents up 40 percent as offices become lofts
contexts.body: Empty office floors are being converted to apartments that rent at the top of the market, and older walk-ups have raised rents to match. Wages for the jobs downtown have not kept pace, so rent takes more than half of many paychecks.

contexts.title: A plasma center in the old department store
contexts.body: The plasma center pays about $40 a visit, more for new donors, up to twice a week. For people between paychecks it is the fastest legal cash downtown.

contexts.title: Night buses end at 11 p.m.
contexts.body: After ridership fell in 2020 the transit agency ended most routes at 11 p.m. Late shifts in hospitals, restaurants and warehouses still end after midnight, so the trip home is a ride-hail or a long walk.

contexts.title: Landlord law: late fees and fast evictions
contexts.body: State law lets landlords charge a late fee of 10 percent of the rent after five days and file for eviction ten days after a missed payment. A short month becomes a fee, then a court date.

contexts.title: Walk-ups with no laundry hookups
contexts.body: Most of the older apartments were built without washer hookups, and landlords have not added them. Laundry means a trip to the laundromat with quarters or a card, several times a week for a family.

contexts.title: Parking where the homes stood
contexts.body: Much of the cleared land became surface lots and a five-level garage for county workers. Residents without a car pay the same meter rates as commuters for a short stop.

contexts.title: Services clustered downtown
contexts.body: The shelter, a free clinic and two meal programs sit within two blocks of each other on Pelham, because other neighborhoods objected to them. People who need them stay close, and their days are organized around intake hours.

contexts.title: Doubling up
contexts.body: To keep up with rent, many households here are two or three earners on one lease: roommates, adult children, cousins. Each owes a share to whoever holds the lease, often by app the night before rent is due.

example.title: Missed the last Route 3 bus
example.body: A dinner shift ran late. The last bus had left at 11:04, so the walk home was 40 minutes in the dark.

example.title: Ride home after a closing shift, $17.40
example.body: No bus after 11. The fare is most of an hour's pay.

example.title: Rent payment came up $180 short
example.body: Rent went up $140 in January. The landlord's portal took a partial payment and added the late fee.

example.title: Rent share sent to the leaseholder, $425
example.body: Three roommates on a two-bedroom lease. The share goes by app the night before rent is due.

example.title: Two loads at the laundromat, $11.50
example.body: Wash and dry for a family of four, twice a week.

example.title: A night at the Pelham shelter
example.body: Intake opens at 7. A bed is held only for people inside by 8.

example.title: Plasma donation paid, $45
example.body: The second visit this week. Paid onto a prepaid card the same day.

example.title: Meter on Pelham, $3.00
example.body: Twenty minutes to drop off a form at the county building.

R1.name: Late-fee ladder
R1.text: A short month means a partial rent payment. The late fee makes next month's bill bigger, so the next payment is more likely to fall short too.
links: Less rent paid in full means more short payments.
More short payments mean more late fees.
More fees owed leave less to pay rent in full.

drivers.t: State law allows a 10% fee after five days.
Rising rents make full payment harder.

B1.name: Doubling up
B1.text: When rent outruns one paycheck, a household takes on a roommate or a relative. The shared lease closes the gap, which holds the late-fee ladder back, at the cost of space.
links: A bigger gap means more roommates.
More roommates mean more shares paid in.

drivers.t: Rents up 40% since 2018 widen the gap.

blocks.name: Larkin Avenue
blocks.summary: Red-rated in 1938, split by the interstate spur in 1961, and left with check cashers when the branches closed.

contexts.title: Rated “hazardous” on the 1938 appraisal map
contexts.body: A federal appraisal map graded the Larkin Avenue blocks red, citing the race of residents and the age of the housing. For decades lenders treated red-rated blocks as too risky for mortgages and deposits, so home ownership, equity and bank branches stayed thin here.

contexts.title: Halvern Works closes
contexts.body: The stamping plant at the north end of the district closed in 1983. Its union jobs paid enough to own a house on one income. What replaced them was warehouse, retail and care work, most of it hourly.

contexts.title: The interstate spur goes through
contexts.body: The state routed an interstate spur through the red-rated blocks, where land was cheapest and residents had the least say. It cleared about 300 homes and split the district. The nearest walkable crossing is now 0.6 miles from the Route 6 stop.

contexts.title: Cutler Run floodplain
contexts.body: A third of the blocks by the creek sit in the 100-year floodplain. Homes with a mortgage there must carry flood insurance, a bill most of the city never sees. These were the cheapest lots, and the ones red-rated buyers could get.

contexts.title: Highway air
contexts.body: Homes beside the spur breathe more traffic exhaust. Childhood asthma is higher here than in the rest of the city, and an attack often means the ER rather than a scheduled visit.

contexts.title: The last bank branches close
contexts.body: After a bank merger in 2009 both branches on Larkin Avenue closed. The nearest branch is now 2.6 miles away. The old Halvern Savings building is a check casher.

contexts.title: Hourly work, short-notice schedules
contexts.body: Most jobs open to people here are hourly, with schedules posted less than a week ahead and pay docked for lateness. Income moves week to week, which makes autopay dates hard to plan around.

contexts.title: State rules on check cashing and payday loans
contexts.body: State law lets check cashers charge 2 to 3 percent of a check and lets payday lenders charge $15 per $100 borrowed every two weeks, about 390% a year. A renewal pays the fee again without paying down the loan.

contexts.title: Route 6 service cut
contexts.body: Facing a budget gap, the transit agency cut Route 6 from every 15 to every 30 minutes. Missing a bus now costs half an hour, and a late clock-in can cost part of a shift.

contexts.title: Zoning and the missing grocery
contexts.body: Zoning keeps most blocks residential and allows shops only on the Larkin strip. The last supermarket closed in 2011 and none has replaced it, so daily food comes from the corner market and the dollar store.

2.text: only strip where shops are allowed

contexts.title: An immigrant gateway
contexts.body: Low rents after the plant closed made Larkin a first stop for new arrivals. Many households send money home every week, and many neighbors work and bank in more than one language.

contexts.title: Church savings circles
contexts.body: Several congregations run rotating savings circles. Each member pays in every week and takes the whole pot in turn. With no branch nearby, the circle is the neighborhood’s savings account and emergency fund.

example.title: Flood insurance autopay, $112
example.body: Household 0391’s flood policy drafts on the 3rd. Neighbors two streets uphill do not pay it.

example.title: Missed the Route 6 bus by a minute
example.body: The next bus is 30 minutes out. Walking around the spur to the next stop takes longer. 38 minutes lost and a late clock-in at the warehouse.

example.title: Groceries at Larkin Market, $31.40
example.body: Milk, eggs, rice and bread at corner-store prices. The nearest supermarket is 3.1 miles away.

example.title: ER visit for a child’s asthma attack, $250 copay
example.body: The family lives 200 feet from the spur. The ER copay is the day’s largest health expense in the district.

example.title: Paycheck cashed at QuikCash, $14.20 fee
example.body: A $710 paper paycheck. The bank 2.6 miles away would hold most of it for two days, so it is cashed here, in the old Halvern Savings branch, for 2%.

example.title: Payday loan renewed, $75 fee
example.body: $500 borrowed after a short week in February. The fee is paid again and the $500 is still owed.

example.title: Debit card declined at Dollar Mart, $23.18
example.body: An insurance autopay overdrew the account at 3 p.m. Paid in cash instead, after a second try.

example.title: Savings circle, $100 paid in
example.body: Week 7 of a 10-week circle at Iglesia Nueva Vida. This household takes the $1,000 pot in week 10.

example.title: Money sent to family abroad, $200 plus $9 fee
example.body: Sent from Envíos Larkin, the only transfer counter open after 6 p.m. within walking distance.

R1.name: Fee spiral
R1.text: A low balance lets a payment overdraw the account. The overdraft fee lowers the balance again, so the next payment is more likely to bounce.
links: A lower balance means more payments overdraw.
More fees mean a lower balance.

drivers.t: Pay that moves week to week makes autopay dates miss.

R2.name: Rollover
R2.text: A short week leads to a payday loan. Each renewal pays the fee without paying down the loan, which leaves the next week short again.
links: Less cash left means more renewals.

drivers.t: State law sets the fee at $15 per $100 per renewal.
With no branch nearby there is no small-dollar loan from a bank.

R3.name: Time tax
R3.text: A missed bus means a late clock-in and docked pay. Less pay pushes back fixing the car, which keeps the household on the bus.
links: More bus trips mean more late clock-ins.
More late clock-ins mean more docked pay.
More docked pay leaves less for the car.
Less for the car means more bus trips.

drivers.t: Buses every 30 minutes make each miss cost more.
The spur forces a long walk to the next stop.

B1.name: Circle buffer
B1.text: A shortfall sends the household to its savings circle instead of a lender. The payout covers the gap, which works against the rollover loop.
links: A shortfall means turning to the circle.
Turning to the circle brings a payout.

cross.t: A payout means one less payday renewal.

blocks.name: Fox Hollow
blocks.summary: Dairy farms subdivided after 1994, reached by a private toll road, and run by homeowners’ associations instead of a city.

contexts.title: The dairy farms are subdivided
contexts.body: Two family dairies sold out as milk prices fell and land values rose. Builders platted them into cul-de-sacs of four-bedroom houses, sold with builder financing to families moving out from the inner suburbs.

contexts.title: The Parkway: a private toll road
contexts.body: The state leased the Parkway to a private operator for 50 years. There are no booths: cameras read plates and mail a bill, with a $4.50 administrative fee each time, and the fees double when a bill goes unpaid.

contexts.title: An HOA for every new subdivision
contexts.body: To avoid paying for new roads, pools and storm ponds, the county required each subdivision to form a homeowners' association. Dues pay for what a city would, and an association can fine and file liens.

contexts.title: Unincorporated: no city services
contexts.body: Fox Hollow was never annexed by a city. Trash, recycling and snow plowing come from private contractors billed to each household, and the county sheriff patrols from 13 miles away.

contexts.title: Jobs 13 miles away, two cars needed
contexts.body: Most jobs are downtown or along the interstate, 13 miles or more by the Parkway. With two earners and no bus, a family needs two cars, and car payments and insurance are the second-largest bill after the mortgage.

contexts.title: The reassessment raises escrow
contexts.body: The county reassessed every home last year. Mortgage servicers recalculated escrow, and monthly payments rose about $210 with no change in the loan.

contexts.title: Cul-de-sacs, no sidewalks or bus
contexts.body: The streets were laid out as loops and dead ends, with no sidewalks to the school or the shops. Every trip is a drive, including the half-mile to school.

contexts.title: The activity economy
contexts.body: Children's evenings and weekends are filled with paid activities. The schedule is a status marker and a second job for whichever parent drives.

example.title: Parkway toll by plate, $6.25 plus $4.50 fee
example.body: The camera read the plate on the way to work. The bill comes by mail with the fee added.

example.title: Toll bill returned unpaid, $9.00 late fee
example.body: The bill went to an old address. The fee doubled.

example.title: HOA dues by autopay, $96
example.body: Pool, storm pond, entrance landscaping and the management company.

example.title: Trash and recycling, $38 a month
example.body: Billed by the hauler the HOA chose.

example.title: School drop-off, 25 minutes
example.body: Half a mile, but no sidewalk on the Parkway frontage.

example.title: Swim lessons for the term, $180
example.body: Two evenings a week at the club pool.

example.title: Mortgage payment, $2,340
example.body: Up $210 a month since the escrow was recalculated.

example.title: Second car payment, $512
example.body: The second car is for the second commute.

R1.name: Plate-bill pileup
R1.text: A toll bill that goes unpaid gets a fee, and the fee doubles. The bigger bill is harder to pay on time, so more of the next bills go unpaid.
links: Fewer bills paid on time means more unpaid tolls.
More unpaid tolls mean more fees.
More fees make the next bill harder to pay on time.

drivers.t: The concession sets a $4.50 fee that doubles.

B1.name: Carpool
B1.text: School trips by car pile up for every family. Neighbors trade drop-offs, which cuts each family's trips and eases the load.
links: More carpools mean fewer trips per family.
Fewer trips per family mean fewer school trips by car.

drivers.t: No sidewalks make every trip a drive.

blocks.name: Mill Street, Ashford Mills
blocks.summary: A textile town whose mill closed in 1998; the county jail went into the mill yard and the college became the biggest employer.

contexts.title: Ashford Mills closes
contexts.body: The textile mill that gave the town its name ran for 96 years. It closed in 1998 as production moved overseas, and the mill houses along the river were sold to absentee landlords.

contexts.title: The county jail goes into the mill yard
contexts.body: The county needed a bigger jail and the mill site was cheap and already zoned industrial. It holds about 240 people, most of them waiting for trial because they could not post bail.

contexts.title: Jail phone and commissary contracts
contexts.body: The county contracts phone calls, video visits and the commissary to private vendors and keeps a share of what families pay. A 15-minute call costs $3.15, and money for snacks or soap goes through a deposit fee.

contexts.title: The bus to Halvern is cut
contexts.body: The regional bus that ran to Halvern every hour was cut in 2015. A county van runs twice a day by reservation. People without a car pay neighbors or apps for rides, or search for one each morning.

contexts.title: The college is the biggest employer
contexts.body: With the mill gone, Wexley College employs more people than anyone else in town, and its students fill the rentals near campus. Dining services and housekeeping are hourly work with semester breaks.

contexts.title: Rent-to-own and pay advances on Mill Street
contexts.body: Where the mill workers' shops were, Mill Street now has a rent-to-own store and a pay-advance app's kiosk. Both serve people with thin credit, and both cost far more over a year than buying or borrowing from a bank.

contexts.title: The hospital closes; urgent care stays
contexts.body: The 60-bed hospital closed in 2017 after it was bought by a regional system. An urgent care clinic stayed in part of the building. Anything serious means a 19-mile trip to Halvern.

contexts.title: Families who visit the jail
contexts.body: Most people held in the jail are from Halvern and the county, so their families come in by car or not at all. Calls and deposits are how most of them stay in touch.

example.title: Dining hall lunch on the meal plan, $9.85
example.body: A swipe between classes.

example.title: A 15-minute call from the jail, $3.15
example.body: Paid from the family's prepaid account with the vendor.

example.title: Deposit to a jail account, $40 plus $3.95 fee
example.body: For soap, snacks and phone time.

example.title: No ride found to the Halvern shift
example.body: The county van was full. An app ride would have cost $34.

example.title: Rent-to-own washer, $28 a week
example.body: Week 31 of 78. The washer retails for $640.

example.title: Pay advance, $100 with a $4.99 fee
example.body: Taken out of Friday's check.

example.title: Urgent care visit, $75 copay
example.body: A child's ear infection. The nearest pediatrician is in Halvern.

R1.name: Advance loop
R1.text: A pay advance covers the gap now and comes out of the next paycheck with a fee. The smaller paycheck leaves the next week short, so the next advance comes sooner.
links: A smaller paycheck means more advances.
More advances mean more fees and repayments.
More repayments leave less of the paycheck.

drivers.t: Mill Street storefronts make advances the nearest credit.

R2.name: Distance tax
R2.text: Without a bus, getting to work means paying for rides or searching for one. Paid rides drain the money that would go toward a car, which keeps the household paying for rides.
links: No car means more paid rides.
More paid rides leave less cash.
More cash makes a working car possible.

drivers.t: With Route 14 gone there is no other way to Halvern.

blocks.name: Main Street, Dunmore
blocks.summary: A grain-and-rail town that lost its railroad, its bank and its grocery; the mobile home park was sold to an investor in 2019.

contexts.title: The railroad is abandoned
contexts.body: Dunmore grew up around a rail siding and a grain elevator. The railroad abandoned the branch in 1979, the elevator went to trucks, and Main Street lost the trade that came with the trains.

contexts.title: The park is sold to an investor
contexts.body: The family that owned Prairie View sold it to an out-of-state investment firm in 2019. Lot rent has gone up four times since. Residents own their homes but not the land, and moving a home costs more than it is worth.

contexts.title: The last bank branch closes
contexts.body: The last branch closed in 2016. The two ATMs in town belong to other networks and charge $3 to $5 a withdrawal, and many older residents still pay with cash.

contexts.title: Dollar stores replace the grocery
contexts.body: The independent grocery closed in 2014, a year after the second dollar store opened. Fresh food now means a 19-mile drive, so most shopping is canned and packaged food from the dollar store.

contexts.title: The state pays Medicare premiums for low incomes
lines: pays Part B for low incomes
contexts.body: For older residents with low incomes, the state pays the Medicare Part B premium, about $200 a month. Enrollment takes paperwork that many eligible people never finish.

contexts.title: Medicaid home care rates
contexts.body: Medicaid pays home-care agencies about $19 an hour. Aides earn far less, with no pay for the 35-mile drive between clients, so visits are short and often cancelled.

contexts.title: Thirty-five miles to the hospital
contexts.body: The nearest hospital and specialists are in Halvern, 35 miles on a two-lane highway. A routine appointment takes most of a day and someone to drive.

contexts.title: Aging in place
contexts.body: Most young adults left for Halvern or farther. Older residents stay in their homes, and care comes from a spouse, a neighbor, a church member or a relative who drives in.

example.title: Lot rent, $455
example.body: Up from $310 in 2019. The home itself has been paid off since 2008.

example.title: Cash from the store ATM, $60 plus $4.25 in fees
example.body: The only ATM open on Main Street.

example.title: Groceries at the dollar store, $23.40
example.body: Canned soup, bread, eggs and milk.

example.title: State pays the Part B premium, $202.90
example.body: Enrolled last year after a pharmacist mentioned it.

example.title: Aide visit, 1 hour of 2 scheduled
example.body: The aide had to leave early for a client 20 miles away.

example.title: Drove a neighbor to the eye doctor, 4.5 hours
example.body: 35 miles each way and the wait.

example.title: Car repair, $410
example.body: Without the car there is no way to the clinic.

R1.name: Lot-rent squeeze
R1.text: Each lot-rent increase leaves less cash. With less cash, moving the home out of the park is out of reach, so the owner can keep raising the rent.
links: Fewer able to leave means increases stick.

drivers.t: An investor owner prices to what residents cannot escape.

B1.name: Neighbor care
B1.text: When an older neighbor needs care, others step in to visit and drive. Their help shrinks the unmet need, which holds the load in balance, until the helpers age too.
links: More help leaves less unmet care.
Unmet care turns into more need.

drivers.t: Short, cancelled aide visits leave more to neighbors.

blocks.name: Route 9 Crossroads
blocks.summary: Farm country consolidated in the 1980s, eleven miles from town, with no bus, no pharmacy and broadband that stops at Route 9.

contexts.title: The farm crisis
contexts.body: High interest rates and falling land prices in the 1980s broke many family farms. Neighbors bought them out, and today four operations farm what forty families did. Former farm families stayed on and found other work.

contexts.title: Patchwork work
contexts.body: Year-round jobs are 11 miles away. Many households here piece together seasonal work at the packing shed, small self-employed jobs and gig work, paid irregularly and often through apps.

contexts.title: The pharmacy closes
contexts.body: The pharmacy at the crossroads closed in 2018 when its owner retired and no buyer came forward. Prescriptions come by mail now, a few days late when the mail is.

contexts.title: No public transit in the county
contexts.body: The county has no bus. A volunteer van runs to Halvern once a week by reservation for medical trips. Anyone without a car pays a neighbor for rides to work.

contexts.title: School districts consolidated
contexts.body: The township schools merged into a county district in 2009. Children ride the bus 50 minutes each way, and the district serves breakfast to everyone because so many leave home before 6:30.

contexts.title: Broadband stops at Route 9
contexts.body: The cable line follows Route 9 and stops. East of the highway, internet means a phone plan, which works for deposits and payments but not much else.

contexts.title: Eleven miles to town
contexts.body: The nearest town is 11 miles away and the nearest city 25. Every errand, shift and appointment starts with a drive.

contexts.title: Church ride lists
lines: The church keeps a ride list
contexts.body: The church at the crossroads keeps a list of who can drive when. Rides to work are paid, a few dollars toward gas; rides to the doctor usually are not.

example.title: Ride to the early shift, $10 toward gas
example.body: A neighbor drives three people to the plant.

example.title: Paid for a fence repair, $220
example.body: Cash, for two days of work.

example.title: Mail-order prescription, $12 copay
example.body: A 90-day supply. The last order arrived four days late.

example.title: Instant cash-out, $180 less a $2.70 fee
example.body: Gig pay moved to the debit card tonight instead of in three days.

example.title: Check deposited by phone, $340
example.body: The bank is 25 miles away.

example.title: Breakfast at school
example.body: The bus left at 6:25.

example.title: Drove a neighbor to dialysis, 5 hours
example.body: Three times a week, 25 miles each way.

R1.name: Ride debt
R1.text: Without a working car, getting to work means paying for rides. What goes to rides doesn't go to repairs, so the car stays broken and the rides continue.
links: No car means more paid rides.
More paid rides leave less for repairs.
Money for repairs keeps the car running.

drivers.t: With no county transit, rides are the only option.

B1.name: Ride list
B1.text: When someone needs a ride, the church list finds a driver. The more drivers on the list, the fewer trips go unmade.
links: More drivers mean fewer trips missed.
Missed trips come back as more need.

drivers.t: Eleven miles to town makes every trip a ride.
